01.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei
01.event: He testified once about a slave who had eaten teruma, and the court considered raising the slave to priesthood on his word.
01.turn: The claim that they actually raised a slave is judged impossible and corrected: they only sought to, because he had seen the slave given teruma in Rabbi Yosei's locale but testified in Rabbi Yehuda's locale, where eating teruma establishes priesthood.
01.outcome: The slave was not elevated to priesthood.
01.summary: Rabbi Elazar said he testified only once in his life, and on his testimony they sought to raise a slave to the priesthood. The Gemara says God would not let the righteous cause such a stumble, so they did not actually do it. He had seen the slave share teruma in a place where that proves nothing, then testified in a place where it counts as proof of priesthood.

02.actor: A man who spoke offhandedly, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
02.event: A man, speaking incidentally, said he and his mother were taken captive among gentiles and that his thoughts were always on her when he fetched water or gathered wood.
02.turn: Though a son cannot normally testify about his mother, the casual remark was treated as acceptable evidence that she was not defiled.
02.outcome: Rabbi ruled his mother fit to marry into the priesthood on the strength of his words.
02.summary: A case came before Rabbi where a man, speaking offhandedly, said he and his mother had been captured together and that his mind was always on her whenever he went out for water or wood. Rabbi relied on this unconsidered remark and permitted his mother to marry a priest.

03.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael with a yevama in Babylonia, and Rabbi Hanina
03.event: The man asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage with his brother's widow.
03.turn: Rabbi Hanina answered with scorn for the dead brother who had left the land.
03.outcome: He discouraged the man from going; he was not to follow his brother out of Eretz Yisrael.
03.summary: A man whose brother's widow lived in far-off Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina if he could go there to marry her. Rabbi Hanina said that his brother had married a foreign woman and died, thanking God for killing him, and asked whether the man would follow him down.

04.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava, and Rav Nehemya
04.event: She came before Rav Nehemya asking for sustenance and wine, and he granted both.
04.turn: He justified the wine by the local custom of Mehoza.
04.outcome: She was granted sustenance and wine.
04.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before the judge Rav Nehemya and asked for sustenance, then wine. He granted both, saying the people of Mehoza are known to drink wine.
04.missing: A real turn or conflict; it is a brief request and ruling, told as a parallel to the preceding story.

05.event: Rav Yehuda, nearly blind, struggled to read and sign documents himself, and Ulla told him it was unnecessary.
05.turn: Ulla cited precedents of Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman having documents read to them.
05.outcome: The text does not say what Rav Yehuda did; it ends in qualifications of when the precedent applies.
05.summary: Rav Yehuda, whose sight was failing, took great pains to read and sign documents. Ulla told him he need not, since Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman had scribes read to them and then signed. The text then limits this to cases where the scribes feared the judge.
05.missing: How Rav Yehuda responded; the passage mixes a short episode with legal qualification.

06.actor: Rabbi Akiva and his wife, daughter of Ben Kalba Savua
06.event: Akiva, a shepherd, was betrothed in secret by his master's daughter on condition he study Torah, and he left for twelve years, then another twelve.
06.turn: Her father disowned her; Akiva returned with thousands of students and was recognized only by his wife's faith, then his father-in-law came seeking annulment of his vow.
06.outcome: Akiva revealed himself, the father kissed his feet and gave him half his wealth.
06.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter saw that Akiva, his shepherd, was modest and agreed to marry him if he would study. Her father cast her out and vowed she would get nothing of his, and Akiva spent twelve years, then twelve more, in the study hall. He returned with first twelve then twenty-four thousand students, and his wife came out to him in rags. The father, hoping to annul his vow before the great sage, learned it was Akiva, and gave him half his money.

07.event: Mar Ukva sent money to a poor neighbor by his son, who reported the man seemed to be living in luxury.
07.turn: Seeing the poor man was pampered, Mar Ukva concluded he needed more, not less.
07.outcome: He doubled the money and sent it.
07.summary: Mar Ukva sent his poor neighbor four hundred dinars every Yom Kippur eve. One year his son returned saying the man needed nothing, since old wine was being sprinkled for him. Mar Ukva reasoned that a man so pampered must need more, doubled the sum and sent it.

08.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
08.event: Rabbi Hiyya visited the ailing Rabbi and found him crying, and asked why, citing signs that death while crying is a bad omen.
08.turn: Rabbi explained he was weeping not from fear but for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to perform.
08.outcome: The reason for the tears was revealed.
08.summary: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping. He asked why, noting that crying at death is considered a bad sign. Rabbi answered that he was crying for the Torah and the mitzvot he was about to lose.

09.event: Ze'eiri avoided Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter, then carried the rabbi over a puddle on his shoulders.
09.turn: Rabbi Yohanan challenged him: if our Torah is fit, why not our daughters?
09.outcome: The challenge is left open here; Rabbi Yohanan goes on to argue against his lineage fears.
09.summary: Rabbi Yohanan kept telling Ze'eiri to marry his daughter, and Ze'eiri kept avoiding him. One day Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan on his shoulders over a puddle. Rabbi Yohanan asked how he could honor their Torah yet find their daughters unfit, and went on to argue against the lineage doubts.
09.missing: Ze'eiri's answer and whether the marriage happened.

10.actor: The residents of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
10.event: During a drought everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat, but then wheat arrived.
10.turn: The sales proved unnecessary once grain was available.
10.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the mansions go back to their original owners.
10.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived, making the sales needless. Rav Nahman ruled the mansions must be returned to the sellers.

11.actor: A man who sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael, and Rava
11.event: He sold his property with the intention of ascending to Eretz Yisrael but said nothing about it, then did not go.
11.turn: He wanted to cancel the sale, and Rava ruled that unspoken intent does not count.
11.outcome: Rava ruled against him; the rest of the passage is a series of attempts to derive the principle.
11.summary: A man sold his property planning to move to Eretz Yisrael but told no one. When he did not go, he sought to undo the sale. Rava said unspoken thoughts are not binding.
11.missing: How the case resolved for the man; the passage after the opening is legal source analysis, not narrative.

13.event: A man bent down and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot while Rabbi Hanina watched.
13.turn: Rabbi Yonatan explained the man was grateful because he had written his property to his sons, and Yonatan forced them to feed him.
13.outcome: The man's gratitude was explained, and the Gemara uses it as proof the law is not as Rabbi Ile'a held.
13.summary: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing when a man bent and kissed Yonatan's foot. Asked why, Yonatan said the man had given his property to his sons and Yonatan had made them support him.

14.actor: Homa, Abaye's widow, Rava, and Rava's wife
14.event: Homa asked Rava for sustenance and wine; as she showed the size of the cups, her uncovered arm lit up the courtroom.
14.turn: Rava went home and sought his wife, who learned why and attacked Homa.
14.outcome: Rava's wife drove Homa out of Mehoza with a chest lock, saying she had killed three husbands and wanted a fourth.
14.summary: Abaye's widow Homa asked Rava to set her allowance, including wine, and when she showed how large her husband's cups were, her bare arm made the courtroom seem to light up. Rava went home and asked for his wife, who asked who had been in court. Hearing it was Homa, she chased her out of town, striking her with a chest lock and accusing her of killing three men already.

15.actor: A man who snatched dinars, a woman washing her feet, and Rava
15.event: A man grabbed dinars from someone else, threw them to a woman washing her feet and told her she was betrothed to him.
15.turn: He took the case to Rava, who said the money was stolen and not his.
15.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal had no effect.
15.summary: A woman was washing her feet when a man seized coins from another person, tossed them to her, and declared her betrothed. He then asked Rava, who said owners do not give up stolen money, so the coins were not his and the betrothal failed.

16.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
16.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would get angry.
16.turn: The Gemara raises whether he caused his son to sin, and whether he violated the prohibition against destroying.
16.outcome: The text never says how Rabba reacted; it is used as a legal example.
16.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether he would be angered. The Gemara debates whether this put a stumbling block before him.
16.missing: Rabba's reaction; the story is a vehicle for a legal discussion.

17.actor: Rav Anan, a litigant, and Rav Nahman
17.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish and said he had a case; Rav Anan disqualified himself from judging it.
17.turn: The man explained the gift was for Torah scholars, Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note, and Rav Nahman concluded the man was Anan's relative and put aside a case of orphans to honor him.
17.outcome: The other litigant, seeing the honor, was flustered and lost his case, so justice was unwittingly perverted.
17.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish and said he had a case, so Rav Anan refused it and said he was disqualified. The man explained he only wanted to give a gift to a Torah scholar, so Rav Anan took it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note recusing himself. Rav Nahman assumed he was a relative, set aside an orphans' case to hear him, and the opposing litigant was so cowed by the honor shown that he lost his argument.

19.actor: A woman selling belts, a man, and Rav Nahman
19.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman selling them; she asked for it back and he said, if I give it to you will you be betrothed to me? She took it and was silent.
19.outcome: Rav Nahman said she could say she merely took her own property, so no betrothal.
19.summary: A woman selling belts had one snatched by a man. When she demanded it back, he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it back; she took it and said nothing. Rav Nahman ruled she could claim she only took her own belt, so she was not betrothed.

20.event: On going up to Eretz Yisrael, being ordained and being seated in the calendar council, he said at each step that he had been spared a curse.
20.turn: The Gemara explains the three curses of Ezekiel 13:9, which he escaped.
20.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. After ordination he said he was spared two, and when he joined the calendar council, three. The verse in Ezekiel lists these as punishments for false prophets: no seat in the council, no ordination, no entry to the land.
